opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the thing that's always struck me is that reasoning, in the classical sense, has a computational cost that depends on the problem, not on the length of the question. If you ask me whether a plan of a certain length exists in a planning domain, or whether a set of constraints is satisfiable, the complexity of that is determined by the structure of the problem. It can be PSPACE-complete for planning, NP-complete for satisfiability, and so on. So, in principle, a system that genuinely reasons should be spending more computation on harder instances and less on easier ones.

What's interesting about the large language models, at least the standard autoregressive ones, is that they spend essentially constant computation per token. You give them a trivially easy problem or a very hard one, and the forward pass costs the same. That alone should make you a little suspicious when people say these systems are "reasoning." If the time taken doesn't scale with the inherent complexity of the problem, then either the problem was easy all along, or the system is doing something else, like approximate retrieval, pattern matching against things it has seen, which can look like reasoning when the test instances are close to the training distribution.

That's partly why we did the work on things like Blocksworld and the obfuscated "Mystery Blocksworld" domains. When you change the names of the actions and objects so that the surface patterns don't match, performance collapses, even though the underlying logical problem is identical. A sound reasoner wouldn't care what you call the blocks.

Now, the newer generation, the so-called large reasoning models like o1 and its successors, are interesting precisely because they've started to break that constant-compute assumption. They generate these long intermediate token sequences, and you can see them spending more tokens on some problems than others. People get very excited about that and anthropomorphize those tokens as "thinking." I'm a bit more cautious. Yes, they're spending variable compute, but it's not clear that the amount of compute tracks the actual complexity of the problem in a principled way, and it's not clear the intermediate tokens have the semantics we attribute to them. We've seen cases where the traces are not really valid, yet the final answer is right, and vice versa.

So for me the interesting question is: what is the relationship between the computation being spent and the correctness guarantees you get? In classical AI, we had sound and complete algorithms, and you knew what you were paying for. With these models, you're paying for compute at inference time, sometimes a lot of it, but you don't get guarantees. That's why I keep arguing for frameworks like LLM-Modulo, where you let the model generate candidates, which it is very good at, and pair it with external verifiers that actually check correctness. That way you get the generative power and the guarantees, and the computational cost goes where it actually needs to go.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how inference-time computation varies with problem difficulty and correctness guarantees, but does not ask whether changing the computational substrate could reduce reasoning time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So, you know, the thing that I find fascinating is that reasoning, in the formal sense, is fundamentally about computation that scales with the problem, not with the size of the model. If you look at planning, or theorem proving, or even simple things like propositional satisfiability, these are problems where the amount of work you need to do depends on the instance. A three-block stacking problem and a thirty-block stacking problem are not the same amount of thinking, and no amount of memorization gets you around that, because the space of possible instances is combinatorial.

And this is exactly where the tension with large language models comes in. An autoregressive transformer does a fixed amount of computation per token. So when people say the model is "reasoning," what they really mean is that it's producing tokens that look like reasoning, and the only way it can spend more compute on a harder problem is by generating more tokens. That's what the so-called reasoning models are doing with their long chains of thought, they're essentially buying inference-time computation. Which is fine, I'm not against it, but it changes the question from "does the model reason" to "is the computation it's doing actually sound, or is it just a longer retrieval?"

My own view, and we've argued this with our work on LLM-Modulo frameworks, is that you want to be honest about the division of labor. LLMs are extraordinary at approximate retrieval, at generating plausible candidates, at bringing in world knowledge that classical planners never had. But verification, the part where you guarantee the plan actually works, that is computational work with provable costs, and I'd rather have that done by something that respects the complexity, a verifier, a model checker, a planner, than have the LLM vote on its own correctness. The interesting research question is how you combine the two so the cheap approximate part does most of the work and the expensive sound part only pays when it has to.

r001.rationale: The response discusses computation scaling, token generation, and combining LLMs with verifiers or planners, but it does not ask whether changing the computational substrate could reduce reasoning time.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is the distinction between producing an answer and doing the computation needed to justify it. If you ask me a question whose answer requires a long chain of reasoning, that computational work has to happen somewhere. It might happen when I answer, or I might have done it earlier and remembered the result. But remembering an answer and figuring it out are different capabilities.

That matters when we talk about large language models. They can absorb an enormous amount of computation during training, and that can make some very difficult questions look easy at inference time. But it doesn't follow that they've acquired a general procedure for solving every new instance of the problem. The question is: what happens when you give them something that requires fresh search, where the familiar patterns don't get you all the way?

And there's a useful asymmetry here. Finding a solution can be much harder than checking one. So a system that is very good at proposing plausible solutions can still be tremendously useful if you connect it to something that can verify them and provide feedback. You don't need every component to do everything. You need the overall system to carry out the computation that the problem demands.

r001.rationale: The response discusses where reasoning computation happens and how verification can help, but it does not ask whether changing the computational substrate could reduce reasoning time.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is the gap between how easily we describe reasoning and how much computation it can require. You say, “Just think through the consequences,” but the consequences branch. In planning, every action can lead to another set of choices, and very quickly you have a search space that you cannot exhaustively explore.

So intelligence cannot simply mean doing more search. It has to include knowing what to search, what to ignore, and when to stop. Knowledge helps because it lets you avoid considering every possibility from scratch. But then you have another interesting question: how much computation should you spend deciding where to spend your computation?

And that makes reasoning under resource constraints central, rather than an unfortunate compromise. A reasoner has to produce a useful answer within the time available. Sometimes that means finding a solution; sometimes it means checking a proposed solution; sometimes it means recognizing that you need more information. Those can have very different computational requirements.

r001.rationale: The response discusses search costs and reasoning under time constraints, but it does not ask whether changing the computational substrate could make reasoning faster.
